abstract: The mesopelagic zone (200 to 1000 m) of the ocean represents Earth's largest yet most underexplored biome, particularly with respect to viral diversity and function. The deep-sea virome of the Indian Ocean remains largely unexplored despite the ecological significance of marine viruses in regulating microbial mortality, biogeochemical cycling and carbon flux via the viral shunt. In this study, we explored the diversity of DNA viruses across mesopelagic depths in the Andaman Sea. Seawater samples collected from multiple depths were enriched for viral particles, followed by viral DNA extraction and long-read metagenomic sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies. We used three complementary approaches for the identification of assembled contigs of viruses. Based on the consensus from these three approaches followed by quality assessment, we retained 1,604 viral contigs of high-confidence and high-quality. Among the taxonomically assigned viruses, members of the class Caudoviricetes dominated across all samples. The assignment decreased substantially at lower taxonomic ranks, highlighting the limited representation of environmental viruses in existing reference databases. Gene-sharing network analysis further revealed genomic novelty and showing limited gene-sharing relationships with reference genomes. Host prediction analyses assigned putative hosts to 10.7% of viral contigs, of which 98.3% were associated with bacteria and 1.7% with archaea. Among predicted bacterial hosts, Pseudomonadota predominated. Structure-informed functional annotation of complete viral contigs identified predominantly structural and tail-associated proteins, while a substantial proportion of viral proteins remained functionally uncharacterized. Collectively, these findings reveal previously under-explored viral diversity in the mesopelagic Andaman Sea study and provide the first comprehensive insight into the deep-ocean virome of this region.
